summaries.example: Imagine two switches, A and B, connected in a way that works only when both are on. The statement “A and B” is true only when both switches are on. The statement “not A” is true when switch A is off. A truth table lists every possible on-or-off combination and shows the result.
summaries.summary: Propositional logic is a way to study reasoning by looking at whole sentences and the small words that connect them. We can use letters such as A and B for sentences, then combine them with “and,” “or,” and “not.” In classical logic, each sentence receives one of two values: True or False. A truth table checks every possible combination of values. This helps us decide whether a formula is always true, true in at least one case, or impossible to make true. The system also explains why some arguments work and how circuits can be designed. The entry describes formal proof systems as well as truth tables. It also explains that logicians have developed other systems, including many-valued, intuitionistic, relevance, connexive, and linear logics, because classical rules do not capture every purpose or interpretation.
key_ideas: Propositional logic studies how whole claims fit together using connectives such as “and,” “or,” and “not.”
In classical propositional logic, every claim is assigned one of two values: True or False.
Truth tables let us check whether a statement is always true, sometimes true, or never true.
The connectives not, and, and or are powerful enough to describe the truth behavior of any other classical connective.
Logic can describe switch circuits, because switches can be treated as open or closed.
Other logics use different ideas about truth, proof, conditionals, or available resources.
summaries.why_it_matters: Propositional logic gives people a careful way to test reasoning instead of relying only on how an argument sounds. Its simple True-and-False rules are useful for mathematics, computer circuits, and decision procedures. Studying its limits also shows why different kinds of logic may be useful for conditionals, incomplete information, constructive proofs, or limited resources.

important_terms.definition: A sentence that makes a claim and can be treated as true or false in the classical system.
A word or symbol such as “and,” “or,” or “not” that joins or changes whole claims.
A chart showing what truth value a statement gets for every possible set of truth values of its parts.
A statement that is true in every possible assignment of True and False.
A statement that is true in at least one possible assignment of True and False.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “if A, then B” mean more than simply checking whether A and B are true or false?
Can you make a statement that is true only when exactly one of two switches is on?
Why would a computer need rules for combining True and False?
Should every statement that is not proven false count as true?

summaries.example: Consider the formula “If the alarm is set, then the door is locked,” written A ⊃ B in the classical material interpretation. It is false only when A is true and B is false; in every other truth-value assignment it is true. This makes A ⊃ B equivalent to ¬A ∨ B. But the source stresses that this truth function should not automatically be identified with the ordinary relation of implication or with every use of “if,” since those may depend on more than the truth values of A and B.
summaries.summary: Propositional logic isolates the behavior of connectives that operate on whole propositions rather than on names, predicates, or claims about sentences. In the classical interpretation, atomic formulas receive True or False, and each connective is represented by a truth function. This yields precise notions of validity, satisfiability, consequence, and equivalence. Truth tables establish decidability, while normal-form theorems show that arbitrary classical formulas can be represented in standardized Boolean forms. The connectives not, and, and or are truth-functionally complete, which explains why larger vocabularies can be treated as abbreviations. The material conditional is especially important: its truth function is equivalent to not-A-or-B, but it must not be confused with the relation of implication, and its adequacy for ordinary “if–then” language remains contested. Formal deduction systems, natural deduction, and sequent calculi provide alternative accounts of logicality. Classical systems are complete with respect to truth-functional validity, and compactness says that satisfiability of all finite subsets guarantees satisfiability of the entire set. The entry then compares classical logic with many-valued, constructive, relevance, connexive, and linear systems.
key_ideas: The basic objects are formulas built recursively from atomic propositional variables and connectives of different arities.
Classical truth-functional semantics assigns True or False to atoms and evaluates complex formulas compositionally.
The connectives ¬, ∧, and ∨ are truth-functionally complete; every classical connective can be represented using them, and even smaller complete sets are possible.
Normal-form results transform formulas into disjunctions of conjunctions or conjunctions of disjunctions of literals.

The material conditional has a precise truth table, but the source distinguishes it from the non-truth-functional relation of logical implication and discusses competing analyses of ordinary conditionals.
Classical propositional logic is decidable, yet its satisfiability problem is NP-complete; it is also compact and has equivalent formal proof systems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Propositional logic is a compact setting in which central logical ideas can be made exact: semantic evaluation, formal proof, consistency, completeness, decidability, independence, and computational complexity. It also clarifies a major philosophical issue: a formal connective may be valuable for its role within a logical theory even if it does not capture every pragmatic or inferential feature of its natural-language counterpart. Alternative systems reveal that disagreements about logic can concern truth values, proof conditions, relevance, or resource use.

important_terms.definition: A formal language whose atomic variables represent whole propositions and whose connectives combine those variables into larger formulas.
An operation that maps the truth values of one or more inputs to the truth value of an output.
A formula true under every assignment of classical truth values to its atomic variables.
A formula true under at least one assignment of classical truth values.
A formula or connective set that can reproduce the truth behavior of every classical truth function.
A formal proof system whose axioms and inference rules generate formulas as theorems.
The classical result that a formula is formally provable exactly when it is true under every classical truth assignment.
The principle that if every finite part of a set of formulas can be satisfied together, then the whole set can be satisfied together.

questions_to_think_about: Why does knowing the truth values of A and B not by itself settle whether A genuinely implies B?
Does a truth-functional analysis capture all that speakers mean by an ordinary conditional?
Why might a normal form be useful even when it makes a formula longer?
How does the completeness theorem connect semantic truth tables with syntactic proofs?
What changes when a logic rejects the law of excluded middle or treats information as a limited resource?

summaries.example: Suppose a school club plans an event. Let A mean “the room is available” and B mean “the club has permission.” The statement “A and B” is true only when both plans succeed. A truth table can list four cases: both true, A true and B false, A false and B true, and both false. It shows exactly when the combined statement is true, without needing to know what the room or permission really are.
summaries.summary: Propositional logic examines what happens when whole sentences are joined by logical operators. Letters such as A and B stand for propositions, while symbols such as ¬, ∧, and ∨ represent not, and, and or. In the classical approach, each proposition is assigned True or False, and the truth value of a compound formula is calculated from those assignments. Truth tables therefore provide a systematic test for validity and satisfiability. The entry explains normal forms and why a small collection of Boolean connectives can express all classical truth functions. It also describes formal deduction systems, where axioms and inference rules generate proofs, and shows that classical proof and truth-table validity coincide. Classical propositional logic is decidable, although its satisfiability problem is computationally difficult in a precise sense, and compactness ensures that an infinite collection is jointly satisfiable whenever all its finite parts are. The article also presents alternatives: many-valued logics, constructive or intuitionistic logics, relevance and connexive logics, and linear logic. These systems explore different ideas about truth, proof, conditionals, contradiction, and the use of information.
key_ideas: Propositional logic studies relationships among complete claims, not the meanings of the individual nouns or predicates inside them.
Classical logic uses two truth values and evaluates a complex statement from the values of its parts.
A truth table can test validity, satisfiability, consequence, and equivalence.
Normal forms rewrite formulas into regular patterns made from “and,” “or,” and “not.”
Formal proof systems and truth-table semantics give different-looking ways to describe classical logicality, yet they agree about which formulas are valid.

Logicians disagree about how well classical connectives represent ordinary conditionals and about whether alternative logics are better for constructive reasoning, relevance, inconsistent information, or limited resources.
summaries.why_it_matters: Propositional logic teaches a general lesson about careful reasoning: we can study the structure of an argument separately from the subject matter of its sentences. This makes arguments easier to compare and supports work in mathematics, computing, and circuit design. Its alternative systems also show that “logical” can be given more than one precise meaning, depending on whether the goal is classical truth, constructive proof, relevant connection, or resource-sensitive reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A whole claim represented by a letter, such as A or B, rather than a smaller part of a sentence.
A word or symbol that combines whole claims or changes one whole claim, such as and, or, or not.
A function that determines an output truth value from the truth values of its inputs.
A formula that comes out true for every possible assignment of True and False.
A formula that comes out true for at least one possible assignment.
A formal pattern used to show how a conclusion follows from assumptions.
A method or system of rules for building formal proofs.
A logic that differs from classical logic in its values, proof rules, or interpretation of connectives.

questions_to_think_about: Why is “A and B” a good example of a connective that works on whole propositions?
Can two arguments have the same conclusion but different strengths of logical support?
Why might a conditional that is true whenever its first part is false seem strange in everyday conversation?
What could be gained by using more than two truth values?
How might a logic change if assumptions were treated like resources that could run out?
